newsitem.title: JAPAN: Okinawa governor solemn on anniversary of handover.
newsitem.headline: Okinawa governor solemn on anniversary of handover.

text.p: Okinawa's governor said the 25th anniversary on Thursday of the island's reversion to Japan from U.S. military rule was no cause for festivities while the unwelcome legacy of U.S. bases remained.

"It is not a time to celebrate," Governor Masahide Ota told reporters, signalling disappointment at recent setbacks in his campaign to reduce the concentration of U.S. military facilities on the tiny but strategically located island.
Ota, who has set a target of 2015 for the removal of the bases, said in an interview that the continued presence of U.S. bases cast doubt on Japan's sovereignty.
"We wonder if Japan is really a sovereign country because if it was it wouldn't allow such a thing," Ota told Reuters.

Faced with smouldering opposition to the heavy U.S. military presence on the subtropical island over 1,500 km (1,000 miles) southwest of Tokyo, Okinawa authorities and central government opted not to commemorate the 1972 handover.
Anti-base activists, however, seized on the day to rally for the withdrawal of the bases, which they say stifle Okinawan economic growth and exposes residents to danger, noise and crime.
Amid tightened security around the U.S. bases, several thousand Okinawans took part in anti-base protests, which passed without serious clashes.

The anniversary of the restoration of Japanese sovereignty fell a day after central government leases on land for 12 U.S. military facilities on Okinawa expired but were forcibly renewed over the opposition of 3,000 anti-base landowners.
Ota told reporters he was sorry about being unable to stop Japan's legislature from revising land laws last month to enable the government to continue providing the land for use by U.S. forces.
"I apologise for not fulfilling the expectations of the people of Okinawa regarding the resolution of the land lease problem," he said.
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters he hoped economic progress would win over the disgruntled islanders.

"I will do my best to promote the economy of the island. And, while faithfully enacting the accords of the Special Action Committee on Okinawa, I would like to gain the cooperation of the people of Okinawa by lightening their load even by just a little," he said.

Governor Ota seized on island-wide protests following the September 1995 gang rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen to press for the complete withdrawal of U.S. forces from the island. The men are serving prison sentences.
Okinawa was the scene of the last and bloodiest Pacific theatre battle of World War Two during which a third of the population was killed.

Through 27 years of U.S. rule after the end of the war and the subsequent quarter century, anti-base sentiment has remained high in Japan's poorest prefecture, which hosts about half of the 47,000 U.S. troops stationed in Japan.
Ota said economic reliance on the U.S. military presence for jobs and base rent money was a dilemma facing Okinawans.
"Part of the problem lies with the dependency of many of the people of the prefecture on income from the bases," he said.
